title: Hybrid stream surface and tool slimming PRD (wip)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working PRD sketch for a lightweight, hybrid streaming surface for the Hosted API that reduces tool-handshake bandwidth ("tool slimming") while preserving ergonomic SDK flows for common developer patterns (progressive text, tool calls, and structured fragments). Aim: reduce median client-observed tail latency for small interactive flows and cut average tool-call bytes by ~40% on real apps.

Context / why now:
- Customers are building chat assistants that interleave rapid UI updates and frequent tool calls (search, calendar, DB queries).
- Current streaming model sends full tool schemas and large checkpoints repeatedly when a single atomic action is invoked. That increases bytes and client parsing work, especially on mobile/edge.
- SDK authors are implementing complex client-side logic to synthesize partial outputs, which results in duplicated code and brittle integrations.

Problem statement:
- High per-call payload for tool handshake and structured output frames inflates latency in constrained networks.
- SDK ergonomics vary across languages; teams resort to ad-hoc rehydration, leading to fragmentation and subtle bugs around resume/replay semantics.
- When fallback (text-only) paths are required, clients often mis-handle incomplete frames and produce inconsistent UX.

Goals (measurable):
- Reduce average tool-handshake payload by 35–50% for common flows (measured on synthetic mobile trace).
- Provide a single minimal SDK surface (JS + Python) that handles progressive text + tool frames with deterministic resume semantics.
- Maintain compatibility with existing typed-frame contracts (no forced server-side migration for customers).
- Add per-request latency budget hints so runtime can prefer low-cost variants (e.g., quantized small model) when the developer specifies a sub-200ms SLO.

Non-goals:
- Not a migration of the full typed-tool schema v2. This is an ergonomic surface and optimization layer, not a schema redesign.
- Not covering multi-turn canonical eval framework or long-retention observability (that remains in Optimize/Console).

High-level approach (hybrid surface + tool slimming):
1) Hybrid frames: combine streaming token deltas (progressive text) with compact event frames for tool lifecycle events. Event frames are intentionally small and often only carry ids + pointers to a server-side manifest.
   - Example event frame: {event: "tool.call.start", id: "t-8392", tool_id: "search:v1", arg_ref: "a-112"} (we send references, not full blobs).
2) Server manifest: a short-lived manifest object (server-side) containing full tool schema and recent arg payloads; clients request manifest entries on-demand (only if they need full shape). Manifests are cached on the server and addressable via short ids (base62) to keep frames tiny.
3) Slim handshake: initial session creation may carry the complete manifest; subsequent tool calls refer to manifest ids and diffs.
4) SDK helper: provide an SDK-level rehydration helper that resolves manifests, auto-fetches on demand, and exposes a pluggable serializer for small clients (e.g., favor JSON-lines vs compact protobuf).

Developer experience: SDK ergonomics notes
- Primary flow: simple streaming generator returned from API with on('partial') and on('action') callbacks. Each action callback receives a small object {id, kind, state, previewText?}, plus an awaitable handle.resolve(args).
- Default: clients see a previewText for tool calls (so UIs can optimistically show a placeholder). The full tool args are fetched lazily if the developer calls handle.resolve.
- Resume semantics: SDK stores a minimal local oplog (id, lastTokenIndex, manifestRefs). On reconnect, SDK resends a compact resume token and asks server for frames since token. No full transcript resend required.

API sketch (informal):
- POST /v1/sessions (create session): returns session_id, initial_manifest_id (optional), minimal config.
- POST /v1/sessions/:id/stream (open streaming SSE/websocket): yields mixed frames: TEXT_DELTA, EVENT_FRAME(refs), CHECKPOINT_HINT(manifest refs)
- GET /v1/manifests/:mid (returns schema or payload blob) – TTL 30s–5min depending on plan.

Bandwidth examples (estimates):
- Current model: tool-call frame ~1.8KB (full tool schema + arg).
- Proposed slim frame: ~160–350B (id + small metadata). Manifest fetch (when needed): 900–1400B but happens rarely and can be cached across calls. Net savings depends on cache hit rate; with moderate reuse, net per-call bytes drop >40%.

Latency budgeting and runtime hints:
- New optional header: X-Redwood-Latency-Budget: <ms> used by smart routing and cost heuristics. If budget < 200ms, runtime prefers local manifest caches, smaller models, and synchronous fallback disabled.
- SDK surfaces budget as an option on session create and per-call override.

Structured output and graceful fallback:
- Structured frames remain first-class: structured fragments are emitted as compressed JSON-lines or CBOR-lite depending on client preference.
- Fallback policy: when structured frame cannot be produced (model divergence), runtime emits a special PARTIAL_STRUCTURED frame with an attached fidelity score and a short human-friendly summary. SDK layers unify this into a single callback so UIs can either show the summary or open a resolve flow.

Edge/mobile considerations:
- Provide a "slim serializer" in JS SDK that uses compact keys and base64 blobs for attachments. Mobile clients can request manifest pruning at session startup to avoid fetching rarely used tool schemas.
- Offer optional delta compression for repeated argument objects across a session.

Operational implications / server-side changes (sketch):
- Short-lived manifest store (in-memory + Redis backing) with eviction by usage. Need metrics: manifest hit rate, average manifest size, bytes saved, extra GET latency.
- Instrumentation on frame sizes per-request and latency breakouts for manifest fetch.
- Opt-in rollout: start with dedicated beta customers and a toggle in Console (enable hybrid-surface) per project.

Metrics to track (success criteria):
- client_observed_ttfb (median) for interactive flows (goal: -20% over baseline).
- per_tool_call_bytes (median) (goal: -35%).
- manifest_hit_rate (target: >60% on typical assistant sessions).
- client_resume_success_rate (target: >99.5%).

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (internal): prototype JS SDK sampler + runtime manifest store. Smoke test with internal integrations. 3 weeks.
- Phase 1 (alpha): expose to 3 beta customers, enable with console toggle, collect metrics. 6 weeks.
- Phase 2 (wider beta): add Python SDK ergonomics, mobile serializer, refine protocol. 8 weeks.
- Phase 3 (GA): expose hybrid surface by default with opt-out toggle. 4 weeks stabilization.

Open questions / risks (todo):
- Security: do manifests leak sensitive data? Need clear rules and opt-in for secrets in manifests.
- Cache consistency: how to guarantee manifest id freshness when tool schemas change mid-session? Consider include-version and manifest invalidation semantics.
- Client complexity: are lazy fetch semantics confusing for developers? We need very good SDK defaults and small examples.
- Long-tail devices: Will manifest GET latency on cold mobile networks offset savings? Need experiments with CDN placement and manifest prefetch heuristics.

Next steps / immediate action items:
- [ ] engineering spike: basic manifest store + server refs (owner: Connor). 1 week.
- [ ] JS SDK prototype: streaming generator + slim serializer (owner: Priya). 2 weeks.
- [ ] Design: UX patterns for previewText + resolve flows (owner: Elena). 1 week.
- [ ] Security review: policy for manifests and TTL defaults (owner: Gabriel). 1 week.

Notes to reviewers:
- This draft intentionally sketches a pragmatic hybrid instead of a full schema rewrite. We're trying to minimize code churn for existing customers while enabling clear gains for mobile and high-frequency tool apps.
- Feedback specifically wanted on: manifest TTL ranges, resume token size limits, and ideal SDK callback ergonomics for the JS streaming generator.

Appendix: quick example JS usage (sketch):
const session = await Redwood.createSession({latencyBudgetMs: 180});
const stream = await session.openStream();
stream.on('partial', t => renderText(t));
stream.on('action', async a => {
  showToolPreview(a.previewText);
  if (shouldResolve(a)) {
    const args = await a.resolve.fetchArgsIfNeeded(); // downloads manifest only when needed
    const result = await localTool.run(args);
    await a.resolve.complete({output: result});
  }
});

(End of draft)
